title: How Many? fields are seeded per player, not per round, so players see different counts and the H3 reveal plots most guesses against someone else's true count
evidence: The shell sets the game seed to `${round.id}:${playerRowId}` (src/player/PlayerApp.tsx:250 and the fallback at :355). HowMany passes that seed straight to `fieldFor(seed, i)` (src/games/how-many/HowMany.tsx:213, field.ts `Rng("<seed>:hm:round<i>")`). docs/games/how-many.md §2 says "Everyone in a round sees the same three fields", ADR-134 (2) / games-v3.md line 17 say "everyone in the round sees the same content", and src/host/howManyStrips.ts:55-89 relies on it: it takes the MODE of all rows' true_count as the strip centre ("everyone shares the round's seed, so one tampered row can't move the axis") and plots every guess against that one count. Scratch experiment (fieldFor for one round id with six player ids) gives counts [[15,23,53],[9,34,64],[8,32,53],[15,31,51],[12,21,59],[9,35,55]]: every player has different counts. With 7/14/27 possible values per band, the mode is mostly just the first row's count (ties go to the first row), so on H3 a player who counted their own 64 perfectly shows up far off a centre of 53, and the crowd average means nothing. The phone-side rule of never showing true counts "because the whole room shares them" (ADR-136 (3)) rests on the same wrong assumption. The per-player seed was deliberate for Trivia's per-player draw (games/trivia.md), which is why the shell does it. Host tests (howManyStrips.test.ts, HowManyReveal.test.tsx) always use the same true_count for every row, so they never catch it. This is outside the pure timing scope, but it breaks How Many?'s whole reveal flow.
expected: Every phone in one round draws the same three fields (same N_i), so the H3 strip centre is the real true count for every dot.
actual: Each phone draws its own N_i from `${roundId}:${playerRowId}`. The reveal picks one player's count as the centre and plots the others' guesses against it.
repro: Play one How Many? round with 2 or more phones. Compare raw.rounds[i].true_count across the score rows (they differ), then look at H3: dots sit off-centre even for accurate players.
suggested_fix: Give games a shared per-round seed. Either add a `roundSeed` (round.id) prop to GameProps and use it in fieldFor, or have How Many? (and the other games that say "everyone sees the same content": close_brackets, color_clash, swipe_sort, pairs) strip the player part of the seed. Keep Trivia per-player. Add a test that two different player seeds in one round give the same fieldFor counts, and a howManyStrips test with mixed true_counts.
verify_reasoning: Verified by direct code reading. src/player/PlayerApp.tsx line 250 sets seed = `${round.id}:${playerRowId}` at round begin (and the GameScreen prop fallback at line 355 repeats the same pattern). src/games/how-many/field.ts's fieldFor(seed, i) feeds that seed straight into new Rng(`${seed}:hm:round${i}`) with no stripping of the player component, so N_i, the chosen cells and every chevron differ per player even within the same round. This directly contradicts field.ts's own doc comment ('Everyone in a round sees the same field; a reload computes the same one again') and docs/games/how-many.md section 2 ('Everyone in a round sees the same three fields'). src/host/howManyStrips.ts's modeOf() then takes the most common true_count across rows as the strip centre and plots every row's guess against that one value, exactly as described -- meaningless once true_count varies per player. Real, high-impact defect, consistent with the reporter's own top-line summary and with ADR-134's seeding requirement for these shared-content games.
corrected_details: Line 250 citation is exact; no corrections needed.

title: The intro is never persisted or anchored: a reload during the 1.5 s intro restarts it from mount and pushes the round past worstCaseMs; a reload in 'locked' also adds the reload time
evidence: The intro effect (HowMany.tsx:312-316) arms setTimeout(startLook(0), HM_INTRO_MS) from mount, not from roundStartEpoch. onProgress is first called in startLook, so the shell's gameSnapshot stays null through the intro (PlayerApp.tsx:251 clears it at begin). A reload during the intro mounts initialSnapshot() and replays the full 1.5 s after the page comes back. Scratch: reload at roundStart+1.4 s with a 2 s page load -> first lookStartEpoch = roundStart+4900 (vs +1500); idle round durationMs = 42 400 > worstCaseMs 40 000 (docs/SCORING.md §2, how-many.md §3 '39 s'; .claude/rules/games.md 'Never exceed the documented worst-case duration'). The same happens in 'locked' after a reload: runDue fires at mount (timer 0 ms, confirmed) and startLook uses Date.now(), so the next look starts at mount. Scratch: a snapshot with lockedEnd 3 s in the past -> lookStart - lockedEnd = 3000. look/flash/answer resume on their stored epochs, but intro and locked don't, so each reload in those phases adds its load time. Everything stays well inside the 120 s cap, so this only breaks the documented worst case and ADR-018's 'a reload never resets a clock' (the intro clock resets). how-many.md §9 has no 'Reload during intro' row.
expected: The first look starts at roundStartEpoch + 1500 whatever the reloads. The snapshot is persisted at intro start (as games.md says: 'persist ... after every start'). Round length stays at or under worstCaseMs apart from genuine lateness.
actual: A reload during the intro replays 1.5 s from mount, and a reload in locked starts the next look at mount, so the reload time is added to the round.
repro: vi.setSystemTime(ROUND_START + 3400); render with snapshot null; advance 1500 -> lookStartEpoch = ROUND_START + 4900; advance to the end -> durationMs 42 400.
suggested_fix: Arm the intro timer for max(0, roundStartEpoch + HM_INTRO_MS - Date.now()). Optionally call onProgress(initialSnapshot) at mount. For 'locked', starting the look at mount is acceptable (it must not skip the look), but document it. Add a 'Reload during intro' row to how-many.md §9 and tests for a reload in intro and in locked after lockedEndEpoch (today's test covers lockedEnd-200 only).
verify_reasoning: Verified by code reading and by tracing the reporter's arithmetic. The intro effect (HowMany.tsx lines 312-316) is `if (state.phase !== 'intro') return; const timer = window.setTimeout(() => startLook(0), HM_INTRO_MS);` -- armed unconditionally for the full 1500ms from mount, never computed relative to roundStartEpoch. Critically, nothing persists a snapshot while phase is 'intro': commit()/onProgress is only ever called from startLook/startAnswer/lock, and PlayerApp.tsx's round-begin effect sets gameSnapshot: null (line 251) with nothing writing to it until the game itself calls onProgress. So a reload during HowMany's own 1.5s intro card finds local.gameSnapshot still null, HowMany mounts via initialSnapshot() (phase 'intro') again, and the 1.5s timer restarts from the NEW mount time (i.e., from after the reload's own load time), not from roundStartEpoch. Traced the reporter's example: reload at roundStart+1.4s with a 2s page load -> mount at roundStart+3.4s -> first lookStartEpoch = roundStart+4900 (vs the intended +1500); an otherwise-idle player then finishes at roundStart+4900+3*(1000+1000+10000+500) = roundStart+42400, exceeding the documented worstCaseMs of 40000 (docs/SCORING.md worst case, how-many.md section 3's '39 s'), and violating .claude/rules/games.md's 'Never exceed the documented worst-case duration' and ADR-018's 'a reload never resets a clock'. The related 'locked' sub-claim is also confirmed by code: startLook (lines 238-252) always sets lookStartEpoch: Date.now(), i.e. mount/resume time, not an epoch anchored on lockedEndEpoch; runDue's 'locked' branch (line 347-350) calls startLook the moment runDue executes, which for an overdue resume (reload landing after lockedEndEpoch already passed) happens at mount. This breaks the file's own otherwise-consistent pattern of anchoring every other phase transition (flash reload, look-ended reload) on the stored epoch rather than on the current wall-clock time, exactly as the finding describes -- and is a real, if low-severity, inconsistency with ADR-018.
corrected_details: Confirmed as described; the math and line references check out. Note the low severity is appropriate: the round cap is 120s and this never approaches it, so no round is forcibly cut off -- the defect is a violation of the documented worst-case invariant and of ADR-018's resume-without-clock-reset principle, not a functional break.

title: While phase='flash' and flashStartEpoch is still null, no deadline exists; if the page freezes in that window the field shows a full 1 s after the screen is unlocked
evidence: runDue sets phase 'flash' with flashStartEpoch null through setState only (no onProgress, lines 335-337). The epoch is written later by the passive effect at lines 319-322. dueEpoch (line 116) returns null for flash with a null epoch, so neither the scheduler nor the visibilitychange handler (lines 368-374, runDue -> false) can end it. If iOS freezes the page between that setState and the passive effect (one render and commit of 8-70 SVG chevrons, often 16-60 ms on a low-end phone), the effect runs on resume: flashStartEpoch = the unlock time, the field shows a full 1 s AFTER the unlock, and answerStartEpoch = that + 1000. The round is stretched by the whole lock. This contradicts how-many.md §9 'Screen lock during the flash: on return the field is hidden at once'. The window is small but it's the only state with no deadline. It never stalls for good, because the effect always runs eventually. On-screen flash length in the normal path is about 1000 ms plus one render (the effect runs after the paint and the unmount timer is anchored on that epoch), so the '1.0 s' claim holds within a frame.
expected: The flash deadline is known from the moment phase becomes 'flash', so a return from a lock always hides the field at once.
actual: Between the setState and the passive effect, flash has no deadline. A freeze in that window replays the full 1 s flash after the unlock.
repro: Analytical (jsdom's act() flushes the effects synchronously, so the window can't be reproduced without mocking the React scheduler).
suggested_fix: In dueEpoch, treat a null flashStartEpoch as lookStartEpoch + HM_LOOK_MS + HM_FLASH_MS (the latest allowed end). Or record flashStartEpoch = Date.now() in runDue itself and keep the post-commit write only as a refinement. Persist the flash phase with onProgress.
verify_reasoning: The described code shape is real: runDue's 'look'-to-'flash' transition (lines 332-337) sets phase='flash' with flashStartEpoch left null via a bare setState (bypassing commit()/onProgress, unlike every other transition in the file), and a separate useEffect (lines 319-322) writes flashStartEpoch = Date.now() only after that render commits. dueEpoch (line 116) does return null for phase 'flash' with a null epoch, so neither the scheduler effect nor the visibilitychange handler can act while that epoch is unset -- this part of the mechanism is accurately described. However, whether a real device freeze/lock can land precisely inside the gap between a React state commit and its queued passive effect (as opposed to before the state update reaches commit, or after the passive effect has already run) depends on React's passive-effect scheduling internals and the browser/OS's freeze semantics, which I cannot verify by static reading alone, and the finding itself admits the repro is 'Analytical' and cannot be reproduced under jsdom/act() because act() flushes effects synchronously. I was not able to independently reproduce or rule out this race from the code and tests available, and no existing test exercises it.
corrected_details: Plausible mechanism, correctly traced through the relevant lines (332-337 for the bare setState, 319-322 for the effect, 116 for dueEpoch's null handling), but unverified as an actual reproducible defect; treat as a low-confidence, low-priority theoretical gap rather than a demonstrated bug unless it can be reproduced with a controlled React scheduler/mocked timing harness.

title: Game seed is per player, not per round: Pairs boards differ between players and How Many? true counts differ, which breaks the host How Many? reveal
evidence: PlayerApp begins a round with `seed: `${round.id}:${playerRowId}`` (line 250, git blame 006dcc49), and GameScreen passes `local.seed` to the game (line ~350). layoutFor(seed) (src/games/pairs/layout.ts) uses Rng(`${seed}:pr:layout`), and How Many? uses Rng(`${seed}:hm:round<i>`) (src/games/how-many/field.ts:55), so every phone draws its own board and its own counts. The docs say the opposite: pairs.md §2 says 'Everyone in the round gets the same board' and §9 'Shared board ... everyone has the same layout'; how-many.md §2 says 'Everyone in a round sees the same three fields'; ADR-134 (2) and ADR-136 (1) say the same. src/host/howManyStrips.ts:89 takes `count = modeOf(true_count of every row)` and relies on 'everyone shares the round's seed'. With per-player seeds almost every row has a different true_count, so the mode is simply the top-ranked row's count (the first value seen wins ties), and every other player's guess is placed against someone else's count by countPos(guess, count). The crowd mean mixes guesses about different fields in the same way.
expected: One seed per round, shared by every phone (e.g. the round id, or a seed column on rounds). That gives the shared Pairs board and the shared How Many? fields the docs describe, and a correct H3 reveal (true count centred, each dot = that player's relative error).
actual: Each player gets a different board and different counts. For How Many?, the H3 strips centre on the #1 player's counts and plot everyone else's guesses against the wrong number, so a perfect guesser can appear pinned at the window edge. For Pairs, the doc's 'shared board / calling out positions' note is wrong (harmless in play, but a doc/code mismatch).
repro: Start a How Many? round with 2+ phones. Compare raw.rounds[i].true_count across the stored score rows: they differ. On H3 the strip's centre number equals the top row's true_count, and the other players' dots are offset by the difference between their counts and that one.
suggested_fix: Choose one: (a) pass a round-level seed to games (for example `seed: round.id`, keeping `${round.id}:${playerRowId}` only for games where per-player variety is wanted, such as Trivia draws); or (b) if per-player boards are intended, change howManyStrips to compute each dot's position from that row's own true_count (relative error per row, strip centred at 0 %) and update pairs.md §2/§9, how-many.md §2/§3 and ADR-134/136. Record the choice in DECISIONS.md.
verify_reasoning: Read src/player/PlayerApp.tsx:250 directly: `seed: `${round.id}:${playerRowId}`` is per-player, confirmed by git blame context and by GameScreen passing `local.seed` straight through. Read src/games/pairs/layout.ts (`Rng(`${seed}:pr:layout`)`) and src/host/howManyStrips.ts (count = `modeOf` of every row's `true_count`, with a doc comment saying it relies on the shared round seed) -- both derive per-player results from this seed. Read docs/games/pairs.md §2 ('Everyone in the round gets the same board, and a reload shows it again') and §9 ('Shared board: Everyone has the same layout... A timed-out board is not revealed') plus ADR-134(2)/ADR-136(1) in DECISIONS.md, all of which assert a shared per-round seed. The mismatch between code and docs is exact and independently reproducible by inspection alone; this is also already corroborated by the project's own PROGRESS.md, which records this exact bug (PlayerApp.tsx:250, per-round seed fix as the first priority) as a confirmed finding from an earlier investigation pass.
corrected_details: No correction needed for the Pairs/How Many? mechanism described. Minor note: the finding's title/scope correctly says this affects all seeded games, not just Pairs and How Many? (Close the Brackets, Color Clash, Odd One Out per PROGRESS.md), so it is a cross-cutting root cause rather than a Pairs-specific bug, but the Pairs- and How-Many?-specific consequences described are accurate.

title: clear_ms uses performance.now() while the 60 s clock uses Date.now(); a phone that sleeps mid-game submits a clear time without the sleep (score inflated, countdown jumps back up at the clear)
evidence: Line 189: `elapsed = perfStartRef.current !== null ? nowPerf - perfStartRef.current : now - gameStart`, then `clearEpoch: gameStart + clearMs` (line 191). The tap guard (line 167), the scheduler (lines 219-232) and the countdown (line 272) all use Date.now() epochs. On phones, performance.now() is a monotonic clock that generally does not advance while the device is suspended (iOS mach_absolute_time, Android CLOCK_MONOTONIC), but Date.now() does. Scratch experiment (fake timers, Date advanced 30 s with performance frozen to simulate a screen lock, then 7 more pairs at 300 ms per tap): epoch time since the board appeared = 34 250 ms, submitted raw = {matched:8, misses:0, clear_ms:4250}, score 1000 (the doc says 1000 is 'out of reach'). The frozen countdown showed 56 s left, when about 26 s were actually left. A 30 s sleep near the end would also let a clear land with clear_ms well under the time really used.
expected: clear_ms is measured on the same timebase as the 60 s game clock. pairs.md §9 says 'Screen lock: the clock runs on gameStartEpoch'. So clear_ms should never be smaller than the Date.now() elapsed minus small jitter, and the frozen countdown should match what was on screen at the clear.
actual: After a suspend, clear_ms leaves out the sleep, the score is inflated (can reach 1000), and at the eighth match the countdown jumps from about 26 s to 56 s left.
repro: Scratch test pairs-exp.test.tsx E3: advance 1500 ms, match one pair, vi.setSystemTime(Date.now()+30000) without advancing timers (performance stays frozen), then match the remaining 7 pairs 300 ms apart. onFinish raw.clear_ms = 4250, score = 1000, pr-seconds = '56'.
suggested_fix: Use perf only while the page has stayed visible: reset perfStartRef to null on a visibilitychange to hidden (or pagehide/freeze) and fall back to the epoch. Or take max(perfElapsed, now - gameStart - tolerance), or just use epoch for clear_ms (ms precision is enough for a 6 points/s slope). Add a unit test with Date and performance diverging.
verify_reasoning: Read src/games/pairs/Pairs.tsx lines 128-134, 189-191, 205-213: `perfStartRef.current` is set once via `performance.now()` when the board appears (line 209) and is never reset on visibility changes (grepped the file and the whole src tree; Pairs.tsx has no visibilitychange/pagehide handler, unlike HowMany.tsx and SwipeSort.tsx which do). At line 189, `elapsed` at the 8th match is computed from `nowPerf - perfStartRef.current` (a monotonic clock) rather than `now - gameStart` (the Date.now()-based epoch the rest of the game, and the doc's edge-case table, describe as authoritative). I ran a live vitest reproduction (fake timers with `toFake: ['setTimeout','clearTimeout','Date','performance']`, using `vi.setSystemTime` to jump Date.now() without advancing performance.now(), which correctly models CLOCK_MONOTONIC/mach_absolute_time excluding sleep) against the real Pairs.tsx component. Result: clearing the board with a 30s simulated suspend after 3 pairs produced clear_ms=11500 and score=940 -- byte-identical to the no-suspend run of the same tap sequence (also clear_ms=11500, score=940) despite 30000ms more real wall-clock time elapsing. This directly reproduces the claimed score-inflation mechanism (a sleeping phone's clear_ms silently excludes the sleep duration).
corrected_details: Confirmed mechanism and score-inflation effect via independent reproduction, though my test's exact numbers (clear_ms 11500, score 940) differ from the original finding's scratch-test numbers (clear_ms 4250, score 1000) since I used a different tap/miss sequence -- the underlying defect and its direction/magnitude class are the same. I did not independently verify the 'countdown jumps from ~26s to ~56s' framing with precise numbers, but the code at Pairs.tsx line 272 (`remainingMs = gameEnd - clearEpoch` where `clearEpoch = gameStart + clearMs`) makes an inflated-remaining-time display an unavoidable consequence of an undercounted clearMs, so that qualitative claim follows directly from the confirmed mechanism.

title: A timeout or round end during a mismatch lock (or with one card up) leaves unfound cards face up on the done board, contrary to §6/§9
evidence: finishNow commits `faceUp: current.clearEpoch !== null ? [] : current.faceUp` and `lockUntilEpoch: null`. Scratch experiment E1: a mismatch tapped at 59.9 s sets lockUntilEpoch = gameEnd + 600 ms. The scheduler correctly uses min(lock, gameEnd) and finishes at 60.0 s (checked at 60 050 ms with 50 ms steps; raw {matched:0,misses:1,clear_ms:null}, no tap accepted after 60 s). But the done board keeps both mismatched tiles `data-state=up`, now un-muted because `locked` is false. pairs.md §6 'done': 'The board as it was (unfound cards stay down)'. §9: 'A timed-out board is not revealed'.
expected: On a timeout or round end, unmatched cards show face down (or the doc says an open card or pair stays shown).
actual: The 1–2 open unmatched cards stay face up with full-contrast icons after the game ends.
repro: Scratch test E1: advance 1500 + 59 900 ms, tap BUG_1 then COFFEE_1, advance 150 ms. onFinish is called once, and both tiles have data-state 'up'.
suggested_fix: In finishNow, commit `faceUp: []` whenever the board isn't cleared (the score doesn't depend on it), or change pairs.md §6/§9 to describe the current behaviour. In practice P6 is replaced by P7 almost at once, so this is mostly a spec mismatch.
verify_reasoning: Read src/games/pairs/Pairs.tsx finishNow (lines 144-157): `faceUp: current.clearEpoch !== null ? [] : current.faceUp` only clears the face-up array on a full clear; on a timeout with an open mismatch it keeps `current.faceUp` as-is, and unconditionally sets `lockUntilEpoch: null`, so the render's `muted={locked && ...}` (line 314, `locked = state.lockUntilEpoch !== null`) becomes false while `up` (line 305) stays true for those tiles. I ran a live vitest reproduction against the real Pairs.tsx: tapped a mismatch at elapsed 59910ms (so lockUntil=60610ms falls after the 60000ms game end), advanced past the game end, and observed `onFinish` fired with `raw={matched:0,misses:1,clear_ms:null}` while both mismatched tiles' `data-state` remained `'up'` (not `'matched'`, not `'down'`) in the DOM after `phase` became `'done'`. This directly contradicts docs/games/pairs.md §6 ('done ... The board as it was (unfound cards stay down)') and §9 ('A timed-out board is not revealed').
corrected_details: No correction needed; file/line citation (Pairs.tsx finishNow, ~line 155) and mechanism are accurate, and I independently reproduced the exact described defect (unmatched mismatched tiles left face-up, unmuted, after a round-end timeout) with a live test run against the actual component.

title: A finger put down during the 150 ms gap is dropped completely, so the swipe that follows on the next chevron does nothing
evidence: handlePointerDown: `if (current.phase !== 'play' || current.itemStartEpoch === null || current.gapEndEpoch !== null) return;` returns before reduceGesture and setPointerCapture, so the pointer is never tracked. handlePointerMove then exits at `if (before.pointerId === null ...) return;` for the rest of that touch, even after the next item goes live. Scratch probe B (scratchpad/ss/probe.test.tsx): correct swipe on item 0, pointerdown (id 2) during the gap, advance 200 ms (item 1 live), move 60 px then 120 px the correct way. Result: correct stays 1, itemIndex 1, and the chevron does not move. A press gives no direction, so a fast player can put the finger down straight after lifting, while the previous chevron is still flying off, and swipe once the colour shows. Lift plus re-press takes about 100-150 ms, the same length as the gap, so presses often land inside it. The chevron neither follows the finger nor registers, and the player loses the item or gets a miss. This is a likely cause of 'swipes not registering'. The doc allows it (§3 'Presses during the intro or a gap are ignored', §9), but that rule costs cadence at the fastest pace.
expected: A press that starts in the gap and is still down when the next item appears can sort that next item, with the 40 px counted from where the finger is at the item's onset. Alternatively, the UI shows clearly that the press was ignored.
actual: The whole touch is ignored. There is no follow-the-finger and no registration; the player must lift and press again.
suggested_fix: In handlePointerDown during a gap, track the pointer with dragItemRef = itemIndex + 1 and call setPointerCapture. When runTimeline brings that item live, re-base the gesture's startX/startY to the pointer's position at onset, so the 40 px and swipe_ms both start at onset and ss.too_fast still holds. Keep ignoring presses during the intro. Update docs/games/swipe-sort.md §3/§9 ('Press during a gap') in the same change and add a SwipeSort.test.tsx case.
repro: Scratch test B: advance(1500); swipe item 0 correctly at 300 ms; pointerdown id 2 at once (in the gap); advance(200); pointermove id 2 by ±60/±120 px toward item 1's side -> last().correct stays 1.
verify_reasoning: Traced the code directly. handlePointerDown (SwipeSort.tsx:189) returns before any gesture tracking when `current.gapEndEpoch !== null` (i.e. during a gap), so no pointerId/startX/startY is recorded and setPointerCapture is never called. When the gap ends and the next item's itemStartEpoch is set (via the scheduler's commit(next) in runTimeline), the finger may still be physically down, but gestureRef.current is still GESTURE_IDLE (pointerId: null) because the earlier pointerdown was ignored. handlePointerMove's very first line (`if (before.pointerId === null ...) return;`) then drops every subsequent move for that same touch, for the rest of that press. The player must lift and press again to sort the now-live item, exactly as claimed. Reproduced by code trace matching the described repro exactly.
corrected_details: Technically accurate, but note this is not an accidental oversight: docs/games/swipe-sort.md explicitly documents this exact rule twice — §3 ('Presses during the intro or a gap are ignored') and the §9 edge-case table ('Press during the intro or a gap | Ignored'). So the code matches the written spec; this is better framed as a documented design/tuning tradeoff (cadence cost at the fastest pace) than an unintended defect, which the finding itself already concedes. Severity 'medium' is arguable given it's spec-conformant behavior.

title: A drag held across a miss moves the next chevron, which it can never sort; the eaten swipe then leaves that chevron stuck off-centre
evidence: handlePointerMove calls `setDrag(step.dx)` without checking `dragItemRef.current === stateRef.current.itemIndex` or that an item is live. setDrag writes `--ss-drag` on chevronRef.current, and after the re-render that ref points at the NEW item's element (key=itemIndex). When the reducer then registers at 40 px, registerSwipe returns silently at `if (dragItemRef.current !== current.itemIndex) return;` (line 161), or at the `now >= deadline` guard (line 164). Nothing resets the offset: handlePointerEnd exits early because the gesture is already GESTURE_IDLE. Scratch probe A: pointerdown at 800 ms on item 0, advance 250 ms (item 0 missed, item 1 live), move +30 px -> item 1 has --ss-drag '30px'; move +80 px -> correct 0 / wrong 0 and --ss-drag still '30px'; pointerup -> still '30px'. The same stuck offset happens when a swipe lands after the epoch deadline but before the miss timer fires (probe C: gesture consumed, nothing counted, no reset). The player sees the chevron follow their finger, then nothing happens.
expected: Per §3/§9, only the item a drag started on follows the finger. A drag that can no longer sort anything does not move the new chevron, and any consumed-but-rejected registration springs the chevron back to 0.
actual: The next item follows a drag that can't sort it, the swipe is dropped with no feedback, and the chevron stays offset up to 39 px until the next drag.
suggested_fix: In handlePointerMove, call setDrag only when `dragItemRef.current === stateRef.current.itemIndex && stateRef.current.itemStartEpoch !== null`; otherwise setDrag(0). In registerSwipe, call setDrag(0) on every early return after the gesture was consumed (item mismatch, gap, past deadline or game end).
repro: Scratch test A in scratchpad/ss/probe.test.tsx (drag started at 800 ms, held through the 900 ms miss, moved on item 1).
verify_reasoning: Verified by full code trace plus CSS. setDrag (line 214, `else setDrag(step.dx)`) writes `--ss-drag` directly onto `chevronRef.current` with no check that `dragItemRef.current === stateRef.current.itemIndex`; SwipeSort.module.css applies `transform: translateX(var(--ss-drag, 0px))` to that element (lines 160/185/196), so the offset is visually real. Because the chevron div is keyed by `state.itemIndex`, once the item advances mid-drag React mounts a fresh DOM node and `chevronRef` is reassigned to it, so a subsequent non-registering move (dx below 40px) from the stale drag pushes the NEW item's chevron. registerSwipe's mismatch guard (`dragItemRef.current !== current.itemIndex`, line 161) and its deadline guard (`now >= deadline || now >= gameEnd`, line 164) both return early without calling setDrag(0), and once a move registers a swipe (or the touch is otherwise consumed), reduceGesture already sets gestureRef.current to GESTURE_IDLE, so handlePointerEnd's own early-return (`before.pointerId === null`) means setDrag(0) is never reached there either — the offset is left stuck. This matches the probe's described sequence exactly.
corrected_details: The existing unit test 'a drag that started on an item that then timed out never sorts the next item' (SwipeSort.test.tsx line 196) covers the score-correctness side of this scenario (correct/wrong stay 0) and passes, confirming scoring is unaffected — but it uses a single large jump move (straight to +80px) that registers on the very first move event, so it never exercises the intermediate `setDrag` call and does not catch the visual stale-offset bug. title: How Many? steps are chained on the moment each late timer fires, so a screen lock pushes the round far past its 40 s worst case

The module's worstCaseMs is 40 000, which types.ts documents as "Never exceeded", and SCORING.md §2 says ≈ 39 s. The remaining two flashes play in full after the unlock.
expected: Either the timeline stays anchored on the stored epochs, so steps missed during a lock close with their timeout rule (E15: "any attempt whose timeout passed is closed with its timeout rule"), or the docs say that a lock delays the remaining flashes.
actual: A 40 s lock in answer 1 gives a 69.5 s round. Longer locks run until the 120 s local cap or the host deadline.
repro: Render HowMany with fake timers, advance 4 s, setSystemTime(+40 s) without advancing timers, dispatch visibilitychange, advance 40 s: durationMs is 69 500.
suggested_fix: Anchor lockedEndEpoch on the answer's end (OK time, or answerStartEpoch + HM_ANSWER_MS on a timeout) and the next lookStartEpoch on the previous lockedEndEpoch. The originally claimed 69500ms is plausible for a different exact intermediate timeline and doesn't change the finding's validity.

title: A round that ends while the phone is still in its P5 3-2-1 mounts the game already ended and submits a 0-score row for a player who never played

actual: A 0 row appears on the round board and the day board, and P7 shows 0 for a player who never saw the game.

title: A missed realtime round-end event is only caught by the 15 s safety refetch, the same length as the 15 s late-accept window, so a late phone's score can arrive after GD007
evidence: STATE_SAFETY_REFETCH_MS = 15_000 (hooks.ts:22) and LATE_ACCEPT_MS = 15_000 (config.ts). The phone's local cap is at seenAt + 3 s + 120 s = started_at + L + 123 s, and the host deadline is started_at + 128 s. For a phone that saw the round more than 5 s late (E26, or unlocked late), and for any force_end, only the rounds UPDATE ends the game. If that event is silently dropped (no resubscribe, so no load() on SUBSCRIBED), the phone learns of the end at the next safety refetch, up to 15 s later. Its insert then arrives at ended_at + up to ~15 s + RTT, which is GD007 (round_closed), and classifySubmitError marks it 'failed' (score shown locally only).
expected: A phone that finishes because of a server round end submits well inside the 15 s window (SESSION_LIFECYCLE §5).
actual: The worst case sits right on the window edge, so the score is lost about half the time in that path.
repro: Timeline: force_end at t. The realtime event is dropped and the last safety refetch was at t-1 s, so the next is at t+14 s. finishNow and the insert happen at about t+14.3 s, plus a 4G RTT of ~0.8 s, giving t+15.1 s: GD007.
suggested_fix: While a game is on screen, refetch the round rows more often (e.g. every 5 s), or poll the round row once the phone's own elapsed time passes a threshold. Either way keeps the fallback well inside LATE_ACCEPT_MS.
verify_reasoning: Confirmed both constants are exactly as claimed: `STATE_SAFETY_REFETCH_MS = 15_000` (src/player/hooks.ts:22) and `LATE_ACCEPT_MS = 15_000` (src/config.ts:30), and confirmed the server enforces GD007 exactly at `now() > r.ended_at + interval '15 seconds'` (supabase/migrations/20260924000003_score_trigger.sql:285-286). Confirmed `useSessionSync` refetches state on realtime 'change' events, on channel 'SUBSCRIBED' (reconnect), on a 15s interval, and on `visibilitychange`/`online` events (hooks.ts:82-106) — so the scenario the finding describes requires a realtime message to be silently dropped without any accompanying reconnect, tab-visibility change, or online-event, in which case the 15s interval genuinely is the only remaining fallback, and its period exactly matches the server's 15s late-accept window, so a phone that missed the round-end event this way can plausibly submit just past GD007.
corrected_details: The finding's core numeric argument (15s poll vs 15s accept window) and code citations are accurate, but its framing ('only caught by the 15s safety refetch') understates that `visibilitychange` and `online` listeners also refetch state and would catch many real-world causes of a missed event (tab backgrounding, reconnect, network drop/restore). The residual gap is real only for the narrower case of a realtime message dropped while the socket stays reported 'SUBSCRIBED' and the tab stays foregrounded/online throughout — a plausible but harder-to-quantify Realtime edge case, not a deterministic code bug reproducible by a unit test.

title: How Many? reveal timeline starts when the component mounts, not at ended_at, so the crowd-average beat is on screen for well under a second (or never) before the 7 s step ends
evidence: The step boundary is anchored on the server's ended_at: schedule.ts:67 `stepEndsAtMs: endedAtMs + ROUND_BOARD_END` (7000 ms). The dot bursts and the mean use delays that count from mount: RevealIn -> ShatterBurst -> useReplay/playBurst `tl.at(delay, ...)` (plays.ts:389). The mean has `delayMs={HM_REVEAL_MEAN_MS}` = 5200 (HowManyReveal.tsx:239, 254) and fades in over 300 ms (playBurst with shards 0: `duration: length/2`, burstMs 600). The reveal only mounts after this chain: adminEndRound returns (~0.5 RTT after ended_at), then `await load()` in act() (loadHostData = 2 sequential round trips), then the H2->H3 ShatterTransition keeps the old screen for 320 ms and mounts the new children at the swap (ShatterTransition.tsx:31-33, 148), then useRoundReveal's fetchRoundReveal (1 more RTT) before HowManyReveal renders anything (it returns null while rows are null). So L ≈ 3.5 × RTT + 0.32 s after ended_at. Timeline relative to ended_at: last flash-3 dot at L+4.4 s, bursts done at L+5.0 s, mean starts at L+5.2 s and is fully in at L+5.5 s, then the step ends at 7.0 s with a 300 ms StepFade crossfade. The whole picture stays up for about 1.5 − L s: about 1.1 s on the local stack (RTT ≈ 20 ms), 0.15–0.65 s over a hotspot to Frankfurt (RTT 150–300 ms), and it never fully appears once RTT ≥ ~0.34 s. After the last round it's the same 7 s (isLast: schedule.ts:51-55), plus the 320 ms H3->H4 fly-in. Host reload mid-step: `firstSeen` is in-memory, the step end stays anchored on ended_at, but the reveal remounts and replays from zero. Its mount delay after the reload (JS boot + auth + loadHostData 2 RTT + serverNow + fetch 1 RTT) is itself > 1.5 s, so the mean never shows. A reload after ~3 s into the step also hides every flash-3 dot, because they need mount + 3.33 s. Docs say the timing is relative to the step: SCREENS.md H3 'Dots burst in track by track within 5 s; at 5.2 s the crowd average … fades in'; games-v3 §5 'inside the 7 s round-board step'. Stop the Clock shares the same mount-anchored schedule, but it has no final beat.
expected: The dots finish and the crowd-average marker is fully visible with a comfortable margin (e.g. ≥ 1.5 s) inside the 7 s step, measured from the step start (ended_at). A reloaded or second host view shows the same reveal state for the same elapsed time (ADR-129 (1) anchoring).
actual: Burst and mean delays count from the moment the reveal mounts, 0.4–1.4 s after ended_at in normal play, so the crowd average shows for about 0.1–1.1 s. After a host reload mid-step it doesn't show at all. This is a likely source of the reported How Many? 'timing' problem on the big screen.
repro: Play a How Many? round to all_finished with the host on a hotspot. Watch H3: the amber mean bar and the 'Crowd average n' legend appear only as the stage crossfades to 'Session total'. Or reload /host 2 s into the reveal: the strips re-burst from nothing and the step ends before the mean fades in.

Pass the elapsed time since ended_at (server now − Date.parse(round.ended_at), from host.offset) into HowManyReveal/StcReveal and subtract it from every slot delay and from HM_REVEAL_MEAN_MS; anything already due shows at once without a burst. Also compress the How Many? schedule so the complete picture has room, e.g. revealSchedule(counts, { totalMs: 3500 }) and the mean at ~3.8 s, leaving about 3 s for the full picture. Update SCREENS.md H3, games-v3 §5 and config.ts together. Extending the 7 s step itself would change ADR-117/129 timing and needs a new ADR.

(2) Inside the step, HowManyReveal's dot bursts and the crowd-average marker are scheduled with `useReplay`'s `useLayoutEffect` firing on mount and `playBurst`'s `Timeline.at(delay, ...)` counting from that call, i.e. wall-clock time since the component mounted, not since ended_at/stepEndsAtMs. HM_REVEAL_MEAN_MS=5200, STC_REVEAL_TIMELINE.totalMs=5000/burstMs=600 (confirmed in config.ts and motion.ts), so the last dot's delay is 4400ms and the mean's fade completes at mount+5500ms, exactly as claimed. (3) The reveal only mounts after adminEndRound's RTT, loadHostData's two parallel-batch round trips, a fixed 320ms ShatterTransition swap (confirmed in ShatterTransition.tsx: 'onSwap: 320 ms'), and HowManyReveal returning null until its own fetchRoundReveal effect resolves. title: One idle/dead/locked phone holds a short new-game round to the 128 s cap: the room waits 85 s (How Many?), 93 s (Swipe Sort) or 63 s (Pairs) after every live phone is done
evidence: decideRoundAction (hostLoop.ts:124-131) ends a round only on `scoredCount >= joinedCount` or `serverNowMs >= started_at + 3 s + 120 s + 5 s` (roundDeadlineMs, line 100). `grep worstCaseMs src` finds it only in the game modules' index.ts and types.ts, so the host never uses it. joinedCount counts every `status === 'joined'` player (useHost.ts:379), including someone who closed the tab in the lobby. A phone that is alive always submits by its worst case (worstCase.test.tsx). One that is locked, backgrounded (iOS suspends JS) or closed never does. Timeline from started_at: every live phone is done by 3 s + worstCaseMs = 43 s (How Many?, 40 000 ms), 35 s (Swipe Sort, 32 000 ms), 65 s (Pairs, 62 000 ms). The time_cap fires at 128 s, then the 7 s board. That's 85 / 93 / 63 s of a frozen H2 board. H2's TimeLeft keeps counting the phones' 3 s + 120 s (roundTimeLeftSeconds, hostLoop.ts:105-109): it shows e.g. '80 s left' at 43 s of a 39 s game, then sits at 0 for the 5 s grace. H2 shows only 'x/y finished' and no presence or names of who is missing (screens.tsx HostRound), so the operator can't tell whether to force-end. This matches the documented behaviour (ADR-014, ADR-017, SESSION_LIFECYCLE E7, SCREENS H2), but for 30–60 s games it is the room-visible 'timing' problem most likely reported.
expected: Once the round's game can no longer be running on any live phone (started_at + COUNTDOWN_MS + worstCaseMs + grace), the room shouldn't sit on a static board with a 120 s countdown, or the operator should at least get a clear prompt to end the round.
actual: The host waits for the flat 128 s deadline whatever the game. With one dead or locked phone, a How Many? round keeps the big screen for 128 s + 7 s instead of ~50 s, and 'time left' reads 80+ s after the game has ended on every phone.
repro: Start a session with How Many? and 2 phones; lock one phone right after the countdown. The other phone finishes at ~42 s; H2 shows '1/2 finished' and counts down to 0 at 123 s; the round ends by time_cap at 128 s.
suggested_fix: This needs a team call because ADR-017 (Accepted, locked) fixes the 120 s cap; propose it in OPEN_QUESTIONS.md. Options: (a) a per-game host deadline = started_at + COUNTDOWN_MS + games[round.game].worstCaseMs + HOST_GRACE_MS, capped at 128 s, in decideRoundAction (the server's 15 s late window still admits stragglers). (b) Without changing ADR-017: after that per-game time, H2 shows a rail hint ('Everyone's time is up: End round') and/or TimeLeft counts down the game's worst case instead of the 120 s cap. Add the missing-player count or names to the rail for the operator.

title: Pairs: clear_ms is computed from performance.now(), which freezes across a real device suspend, letting a bad clear time score near-max and pass the server bound
evidence: Pairs.tsx:206-213 sets `perfStartRef.current = performance.now()` once, together with `gameStartEpoch: Date.now()`, when the 60s board appears, and never resyncs it again for the rest of the round. At the 8th match (line 189): `const elapsed = perfStartRef.current !== null ? nowPerf - perfStartRef.current : now - gameStart;` -- i.e. clear_ms is measured on performance.now() alone whenever the component wasn't reloaded. Per MDN's 'Ticking during sleep' note (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance/now), only Windows browsers currently make performance.now() tick during OS sleep; Chrome/Chromium (crbug 1206450) and Safari/WebKit do not. WebKit bug 225610 (bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=225610, still NEW) confirms the concrete mechanism on Darwin: WebKit's monotonic clock uses mach_absolute_time(), which 'does not tick during sleep' -- and iOS Safari is the same WebKit/Darwin clock family as the macOS case discussed there, so this is very likely to reproduce on the reported iOS/Android real-device symptom, not just in this simulation. I wrote a scratch fake-timer test (not part of the repo) that freezes a stubbed performance.now() across a simulated 30s suspend (Date.now() jumped via vi.setSystemTime, matching real suspended-JS semantics: no timers fire during the jump) while the player keeps playing normally before and after. Result: raw.clear_ms = 4800 while the true wall-clock clear time was 34800ms; scorePairs(raw) = 1000 (max score, vs. the ~940 a correct wall-clock time would have given); validatePairsRaw(raw, 1000) returned null (accepted) because PR_MIN_CLEAR_MS is only 4000ms, comfortably below the corrupted 4800. A second scratch test showed the exact user-visible symptom: the live countdown correctly ticks down through the suspend (54s -> 23s, Date.now()-based) then JUMPS UP to 53s the instant the board clears (clearEpoch is gameStart + the frozen-clock clear_ms) -- matching the previously reported 'about 26s back up to 56s' almost exactly.
expected: clear_ms should reflect the real wall-clock time the player took to clear the board (gameStartEpoch to the moment of the 8th match), immune to any suspend/throttle in between, so the score and the server's pr.too_fast bound both stay meaningful.
actual: clear_ms is measured on a monotonic clock (performance.now()) that Chrome and Safari both stop advancing during a real OS suspend, while the game's own epoch (gameStartEpoch, Date.now()-based) and countdown correctly keep moving. A suspend of D ms anywhere in the 60s game silently subtracts up to D ms from the recorded clear time, which can push a genuinely ~35s clear down into the < 15s 'full marks' band (score 1000) or even below PR_MIN_CLEAR_MS + lock time and get rejected as impossible in the opposite (unlucky) case; the visible effect is the countdown jumping upward the instant the board clears, and the submitted score/raw is accepted by the server (migration 20260925000800) as if it were legitimate.
repro: Scratch test 'a 30s suspend mid-game inflates clear_ms/score to near-max and PASSES the server bound' in <scratchpad>/g4/pairs-suspend.scratch.test.tsx: play ~4s of taps (2 pairs), suspend the fake clock 30s (Date jumps, performance.now() frozen), then clear the remaining 6 pairs in ~2.4s of further active taps. Result: clear_ms=4800, true wall clear=34800ms, score=1000, validatePairsRaw -> null.
suggested_fix: Measure clear_ms purely from Date.now() epochs (gameStartEpoch and the epoch at the 8th match), the same clock already used for gameStartEpoch/lockUntilEpoch/the countdown and everywhere else in this game, and drop the performance.now()-based branch entirely (or at minimum resync perfStartRef to the current Date/perf offset on every visibilitychange/'resume', the way Swipe Sort's runTimeline already does for itemStartEpoch, so any drift is bounded to the gap between resyncs instead of the whole 60s round).
verify_reasoning: Pairs.tsx:209 sets perfStartRef = performance.now() once, when the board appears (alongside gameStartEpoch = Date.now() at :210), and nothing resyncs it afterwards. There is no visibilitychange handler in Pairs. At the 8th match (:189), elapsed = nowPerf - perfStartRef, and clearEpoch is then stored as gameStart + clearMs (:191). Every other clock in the game runs on Date.now(): the 60 s end in the scheduler, the lock, and the countdown at :270-272. So if performance.now() stops advancing while Date.now() keeps going, clear_ms comes out too small by the length of the stop. The countdown then jumps upward at the clear, because remainingMs switches from gameEnd - Date.now() to gameEnd - clearEpoch. The score is inflated: under 15 s scores full marks (PR_CLEAR_FREE_MS). The server check (migration 000800:439, clr < 4000 + 700*misses) cannot catch an inflated value. It can also wrongly reject a real clear as pr.too_fast when the stop pushes clear_ms under that floor. The scratch output (out4/out5) shows clear_ms 4800 against a true 34800, a score of 1000, and validatePairsRaw returning null, which matches what the code does. This agrees with the earlier investigation's confirmed 'Pairs clear_ms leaves out sleep'.
corrected_details: The code follows its own spec, so the spec is where the defect starts: docs/games/pairs.md:48 prescribes performance.now() at pointerdown, and the fix has to change that doc in the same change. The bug is device-dependent. performance.now() only stops during a real OS sleep (a locked phone on iOS/WebKit and on Android/Linux via CLOCK_MONOTONIC; Windows browsers keep ticking). It keeps running in a hidden but awake tab and under timer throttling, so a desktop test with several tabs will not show it; a real phone that is locked mid-game and unlocked will. Besides the inflated score, the same mechanism can produce a false 'pr.too_fast' rejection (clear_ms < 4000 + 700*misses). Fix: compute clear_ms as Date.now() - gameStartEpoch at the 8th match's pointerdown, drop perfStartRef, and update pairs.md §48. Score and bounds are unchanged.

title: Pairs has no visibilitychange handler: after a phone sleep that crosses the 60 s end, the board sits at 0 with taps ignored and no 'Time's up' for up to about 55 s

Board+5 s for 60 s: stuck 55 s, which is later than the shell's local 120 s cap (53.5 s after return), so in the app the cap rescues it first. Board+40 s for 25 s: stuck 20 s. In the regime table (pr-regimes.g2.test.tsx), B2 mid-board +70 s gives 'finished 54700 ms after return' and durationMs capped at 120 s.
